The Senseless Killing of Nathaniel Julies

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Police brutality is in the headlines once more, this time with the senseless killing of a sixteen years old Down syndrome boy in Eldorado Park, that has ignited outrage & tension within the community.

Unique Selling Point:
On Wednesday 26 August, 16 years old Nathaniel Julies, a resident of Eldorado Park with Down Syndrome, left his home to get a packet of biscuits. He never returned home. His life was mercilessly wiped out by a close range shot, from the barrel of a policeman’s gun.
With 440 deaths “as a result of police action” tabled in the 2018/2019 IPID Annual Report (page 42) why has police violence remained unchecked in South Africa?

Summary:
On the night of the killing in Eldorado Park, the police threw Nathaniel Julies into a police van after shooting him, dropped him off at the Chris Hani Baragwanath Hospital and by the time the authorities got to the potential crime site it had been cleaned up and contaminated.

Police contend that Nathaniel Julies got caught in crossfire between gangs and police but locals dispute this because, for one thing, according to them gang violence has been at a low ebb in Eldorado park. In the immediate aftermath of Nathaniel Julies’s killing we speak to the family of the deceased and local people and campaigners to witness the impact of this horrifying event.

On hearing of the circumstances of Nathaniel’s death residents of Eldorado Park took to the streets to protest. On confronting the mass protest, police attempted to stem the tide by arresting local development and economic civil association chairperson Majiet Amiene, under false pretext, calling him to the police station for a meeting and there arresting him. He is currently in police custody. The community believe Amiene was arrested because he is considered a whistle blower by authorities, exposing corruption emanating from Eldorado Park police station, the nature of which includes lost dockets and collusion with gangs.

As well as the Eldorado Park community and the Human Rights Commission we try to get answers from SAPS and IPID to why police brutality seems to be unabated and what they are going to do about it.

Further information:
Eldorado Park residents on Thursday 27 August demanded the removal of police they blamed for the shooting of Nathaniel Julies. Further clashes have broken out on the streets of Eldorado Park between community and police. But IPID has announced that the locals’ target ‘Scorpian’ is innocent, as forensic tests reveal that the deadly bullet did not come from Scorpian’s firearm.

On a visit to Eldorado Park on Friday 28 August, Police Minister Bheki Cele with Gauteng Safety MEC Faith Mazibuko, promised that if the perpetrator of the killing was from the ranks of the police, they would face the full might of the law, “Because we don’t want the police to be seen interfering on the matter. So, we will find a way and we will find the answers and whoever did it will have to face the law."

So was Nathaniel Julies an accidental victim of crossfire between community and police, or was his death a more sinister matter? With social media video footage recording a policeman at the scene saying “I must get my rifle, I'm going to kill” as he took up his rifle… how can South African’s be confident in their so called protectors?

When we spoke to the Human Rights Commission who are busy mediating the situation they expressed their increasing concern about police violence and brutality. They will elaborate for us on two cases that occurred in the last few weeks:
- In the Cape, a 9 year old boy was shot dead during a service delivery protest in his home - where police entered the yard and were asked not to shoot, but they continued firing and shot the boy who died later in hospital from the bullet wound to his head.
- A 34 yr old in Moorreesburg 90 Kms north of Cape Town died after being beaten by police in a police cell.

As of 2019 South Africa adopted compliance to the United Nations' Prevention and Combating of Torture of Persons Act. It is an admirable effort to instill the concept of dignity and respect when police are dealing with suspects, so that the cycle of violence is not perpetuated.
However, within the South African penal system this adoption is challenging to say the least. If someone is sent to prison, and cells are unkempt or toilets don’t work for instance, the authorities are already degrading the prisoner, which is tantamount to torture. Furthermore when that person leaves prison it is argued they won’t want to rehabilitate. As these minimum requirements are generally failed by the SA penal system, the country’s leadership in law enforcement and corrective institutions are not adhering to the spirit of non brutality of the Prevention and Combating of Torture of Persons Act.

So starting with leadership, there appears to be a culture that seems to have been inculcated in SAPS which has to be rebuilt from the top down. Basically, police have to be reeducated about what it is to be a policeman.
The Human Rights Commission has worked with District One police station in the Western Cape to provide alternative dignifying methodologies for handling crisis etc – which has led to turnaround.
Another practical proposal for change is to introduce Body cams to be worn by all officers – to surveille the police, helping to police the actions of the police.

We have filmed the scenes outside Eldorado Park SAPS on Friday 28 August, where locals were not only protesting Nathaniel Julies’s death, but also the arrest of Majiet Amiene who residents say was trying to calm the crowd when police fingered him. We have shot brief interviews with Amiene’s sisters and local campaigner Riaan __.

We will interview Nathaniel Julies’s family, community leaders including Marcelle a special needs specialist in Eldorado Park, IPID and SAPS.
We will also shoot further community protests or marches during the immediate fallout of Nathaniel Julies death.

Press Release:


Enough is enough, say Eldorado Park protesters after one of their own, Nateniël Julies a teen with Down syndrome is killed, apparently in cold blood by a local cop. South Africa’s top brass are with the Eldorado Park community, condemning the killing of Nateniël Julies, promising to seek out justice. Will they be as good as their word?


Script:


Link:On the night of the 26th of August, a 16 year old boy with down syndrome left this house on his regular mission to find a packet of his favourite biscuits. He never returned. //
VO: Nateniël Julies was brutally gunned down allegedly by police officers, in Eldorado Park Johannesburg.//
Posters Justice for Nataniel protest shouts
The community demonstrated their anger against the local police.

Sound up community….

VO: Bridget Harris Nateniel's mother is struggling to come to terms with what happened that night.

Bridget: What I saw with my two eyes,I just I just couldn't believe it, because he was bleeding through his mouth and his nose. He was suffocating his own blood.

VO: On the night of the shooting Bridget was at home with her partner Clint Smith, when they heard a single gunshot reverberate through their neighbourhood.

Clint: I was running out, there was somebody running to the shop I asked that guy. “Hey mey bra! Wat gaan aan?!” He said, “There they shot Nateniël.”
I run back, I say “Bridget come, Bridget come! Me and Bridget ran and the police van already drove up with Nateniël.

VO: They rushed to the Eldorado Park Police station, where they were told that Nateniel had been taken to Chris Hani Baragwanath Hospital. They immediately made their way there, and finally found the doctor in charge.

Bridget: And the doctor came in with a little bit tears in his eyes and he was like the first thing came out of his mouth, is that “Was this a gang fight?”
we say no, it's not a gang fight.
And we ask is Nateniël alright?
And he says “No Nateniël was been shot through the chest.” He is passed on. And there I was like blank, I didn't , I couldn't hear nothing. I couldn’t hear nobody.

VO: Safia Kaldine, an Eldorado Park resident, was standing outside the hospital when she heard police sirens.

Safia: The van came in, and it was in a speed and they just stop by the trauma ward, and as they jump out; The one policeman, grab the boy on his legs out. That it was very ugly.
They just pick him up I mean his head went around, that boy is already dead and they just put him on a stretcher and a police ladies scream help!

VO: Safia, only realised who the boy might have been when the news broke.
Safia: The following day when I saw it over TV When I heard it was a Down syndrome child, that hurts me.

Link: It was at this truck Just 100 metres from his home that Nateniel was standing when apparently a police van drew up and there was an exchange. The details are under investigation. But what is known that Nateniël was shot at short range with a shotgun allegedly by a police officer

Bheki: I went to see the family and the community, which was rightfully very angry.

VO: Police Minister Bheki Cele is deeply troubled by the behaviour of errant SAPS members.

Bheki: So you go back to the question of how then it happens; That people that are paid to defend those people, but they are perpetrators and they killed this person who seems to be completely innocent and completely harmless.

VO: Stories emerged that police claimed Nateniël was caught in a gang crossfire, which enraged residents who were demanding the truth, besides, witnesses had pointed to a policeman known as Scorpion as the alleged shooter. Community Leader Majiet Amien spoke out.

Sound up Majiet:
Eldorado's mense is gatvol, is gatvol, they've had enough.

VO: Riaan Niewenhuys, who works closely with Majiet Amien took us through the scene of the crime.

Riaan: If you can look at that, over there, that would be his prints on the truck. At the time where the police came through and the shooting took place.
Derek: Do you think those were actually his hand marks?
Riaan: That is definitely not a grownup's hand marks but it is hand marks of a child.

VO: Mark Harris, Nateniel's father is tormented by what these trace marks might mean.

Mark: He was standing like this against the truck, So as they did shoot him, he go down.
VO: Community Activist Charis Pretorius is angered by the way the crime scene was mishandled.

Charis: They were supposed to get the ambulance services to come out so that they could then of course, call the forensics team in, secure the scene, most importantly, so that there is no tampering, but the unfortunate thing is none of that was done

VO: Witnesses reported that they saw someone come back to the scene and throw sand over the blood. IPID, the agency tasked with investigating crimes perpetrated by police, acted swiftly, including reconstructing the crime scene, under Executive Director Jennifer Ntlatseng.

Jennifer: The scene was contaminated. And remember, there was a removal of the body by the officers. So we just want to start afresh and see what had happened, we're continuing to interview witnesses, why this boy in particular, what was going on at that particular time when this thing happened?

Derek: Clint it doesn't seem just possible that policemen would shoot a child, so what do you think happened?
Clint: Now if he talked to a Down syndrome child he can't answer you. He is gonna laugh at you.
Derek: But they knew him
Clint: That’s the thing, the police, most of the police knew Lokkie.

Bridget: He was a young, energetic, energetic boy. He was always excited, smiling, greeting people. Dancing was his favorite. [8:00] The week before He passed on, we had a dance here. And he wants to dance better than the sisters and the brothers.

VO: Marcelle Daniels founder of the Caitlin Douman Foundation works with children with disabilities and knows Nateniel quite well, she says he mainly communicated through gestures.

Marcelle: He was very intelligent, if you really had to pay close attention to what he was saying, then you would basically understand the kind of communication that he was trying to get across.
Derek: But he, but he couldn't express himself.
Marcelle: Not like you and I, no. Not if you look at what happened on Wednesday, and he definitely wouldn't have been able to get himself out of that situation at all.

Derek: 11:03 Minister so many cases of police brutality especially during lockdown.in your opinion, just how brutal is our police service?
Bheki: Derek, I, I would really say there is that brutality, but without defending the police. We are in a brutal society, very brutal. Not too many people ask how many police who were shot and killed themselves, which does not then allow police to be brutal to the general public out there as we have seen with Nateniël.

VO: Two Eldorado Park police officers were arrested in connection with Nateniël Julies's inexplicable killing, Simon Scorpion Ndyalvane and Caylene Whiteboy. The message from IPID was clear and on Monday they appeared for bail at the Protea Magistrate's Court Soweto.
Court Link: 00:52 The two police officers face charges of murder, the obstruction of justice and the alleged possession of illegal ammunition

VO: Their bail hearing was postponed till the 10th of September and a third police officer was subsequently arrested, Sgt Vorster Netshiongolo, who is charged with defeating the ends of justice and accessory after the fact, --Murder. The investigation is ongoing and more arrests could follow.
Safia Kaldine says she saw 5 police officers at the hospital on the night of the shooting.

Derek: So there were four police officers and one woman?
Safia: And one woman, because two of us sitting in front, three, the woman in the two were sitting the other two with the other van came in, I couldn't see their faces because it was black.

Jennifer: If police are caught in wrongdoing, we must make sure that we investigate.We need to bring a Community Trust back into the cities to stay. So the very same police officers, who are not doing the right thing, must be arrested, What we need to do is to ensure that justice prevail.

Cele: There are men that are good, but we must concentrate to those that are bad and deal with them decisively and try to uproot them and take them out of the police.

Bridget: I want justice. That's what I want for my boy because the pain he went through. It's unbearable.

So we just want to start afresh and see what had happened, we're continuing to interview witnesses, why this boy in particular, what was going on at that particular time when this thing happened? Derek: Clint it doesn't seem just possible that policemen would shoot a child, so what do you think happened? Clint: Now if he talked to a Down syndrome child he can't answer you. He is gonna laugh at you. Derek: But they knew him Clint: That’s the thing, the police, most of the police knew Lokkie. Bridget: He was a young, energetic, energetic boy. He was always excited, smiling, greeting people. Dancing was his favorite. [8:00] The week before He passed on, we had a dance here. And he wants to dance better than the sisters and the brothers. VO: Marcelle Daniels founder of the Caitlin Douman Foundation works with children with disabilities and knows Nateniel quite well, she says he mainly communicated through gestures. Marcelle: He was very intelligent, if you really had to pay close attention to what he was saying, then you would basically understand the kind of communication that he was trying to get across. Derek: But he, but he couldn't express himself. Marcelle: Not like you and I, no. Not if you look at what happened on Wednesday, and he definitely wouldn't have been able to get himself out of that situation at all. Derek: 11:03 Minister so many cases of police brutality especially during lockdown.in your opinion, just how brutal is our police service? Bheki: Derek, I, I would really say there is that brutality, but without defending the police. We are in a brutal society, very brutal. Not too many people ask how many police who were shot and killed themselves, which does not then allow police to be brutal to the general public out there as we have seen with Nateniël. VO: Two Eldorado Park police officers were arrested in connection with Nateniël Julies's inexplicable killing, Simon Scorpion Ndyalvane and Caylene Whiteboy. The message from IPID was clear and on Monday they appeared for bail at the Protea Magistrate's Court Soweto. Court Link: 00:52 The two police officers face charges of murder, the obstruction of justice and the alleged possession of illegal ammunition VO: Their bail hearing was postponed till the 10th of September and a third police officer was subsequently arrested, Sgt Vorster Netshiongolo, who is charged with defeating the ends of justice and accessory after the fact, --Murder. The investigation is ongoing and more arrests could follow. Safia Kaldine says she saw 5 police officers at the hospital on the night of the shooting. Derek: So there were four police officers and one woman? Safia: And one woman, because two of us sitting in front, three, the woman in the two were sitting the other two with the other van came in, I couldn't see their faces because it was black. Jennifer: If police are caught in wrongdoing, we must make sure that we investigate.We need to bring a Community Trust back into the cities to stay. So the very same police officers, who are not doing the right thing, must be arrested, What we need to do is to ensure that justice prevail. Cele: There are men that are good, but we must concentrate to those that are bad and deal with them decisively and try to uproot them and take them out of the police. Bridget: I want justice. That's what I want for my boy because the pain he went through. It's unbearable.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Police brutality is in the headlines once more, this time with the senseless killing of a sixteen years old Down syndrome boy in Eldorado Park, that has ignited outrage & tension within the community.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: On Wednesday 26 August, 16 years old Nathaniel Julies, a resident of Eldorado Park with Down Syndrome, left his home to get a packet of biscuits. He never returned home. His life was mercilessly wiped out by a close range shot, from the barrel of a policeman’s gun. With 440 deaths “as a result of police action” tabled in the 2018/2019 IPID Annual Report (page 42) why has police violence remained unchecked in South Africa?
metadata.Summary: On the night of the killing in Eldorado Park, the police threw Nathaniel Julies into a police van after shooting him, dropped him off at the Chris Hani Baragwanath Hospital and by the time the authorities got to the potential crime site it had been cleaned up and contaminated. Police contend that Nathaniel Julies got caught in crossfire between gangs and police but locals dispute this because, for one thing, according to them gang violence has been at a low ebb in Eldorado park. In the immediate aftermath of Nathaniel Julies’s killing we speak to the family of the deceased and local people and campaigners to witness the impact of this horrifying event. On hearing of the circumstances of Nathaniel’s death residents of Eldorado Park took to the streets to protest. On confronting the mass protest, police attempted to stem the tide by arresting local development and economic civil association chairperson Majiet Amiene, under false pretext, calling him to the police station for a meeting and there arresting him. He is currently in police custody. The community believe Amiene was arrested because he is considered a whistle blower by authorities, exposing corruption emanating from Eldorado Park police station, the nature of which includes lost dockets and collusion with gangs. As well as the Eldorado Park community and the Human Rights Commission we try to get answers from SAPS and IPID to why police brutality seems to be unabated and what they are going to do about it.
metadata.Further information: Eldorado Park residents on Thursday 27 August demanded the removal of police they blamed for the shooting of Nathaniel Julies. Further clashes have broken out on the streets of Eldorado Park between community and police. But IPID has announced that the locals’ target ‘Scorpian’ is innocent, as forensic tests reveal that the deadly bullet did not come from Scorpian’s firearm. On a visit to Eldorado Park on Friday 28 August, Police Minister Bheki Cele with Gauteng Safety MEC Faith Mazibuko, promised that if the perpetrator of the killing was from the ranks of the police, they would face the full might of the law, “Because we don’t want the police to be seen interfering on the matter. So, we will find a way and we will find the answers and whoever did it will have to face the law." So was Nathaniel Julies an accidental victim of crossfire between community and police, or was his death a more sinister matter? With social media video footage recording a policeman at the scene saying “I must get my rifle, I'm going to kill” as he took up his rifle… how can South African’s be confident in their so called protectors? When we spoke to the Human Rights Commission who are busy mediating the situation they expressed their increasing concern about police violence and brutality. They will elaborate for us on two cases that occurred in the last few weeks: - In the Cape, a 9 year old boy was shot dead during a service delivery protest in his home - where police entered the yard and were asked not to shoot, but they continued firing and shot the boy who died later in hospital from the bullet wound to his head. - A 34 yr old in Moorreesburg 90 Kms north of Cape Town died after being beaten by police in a police cell. As of 2019 South Africa adopted compliance to the United Nations' Prevention and Combating of Torture of Persons Act. It is an admirable effort to instill the concept of dignity and respect when police are dealing with suspects, so that the cycle of violence is not perpetuated. However, within the South African penal system this adoption is challenging to say the least. If someone is sent to prison, and cells are unkempt or toilets don’t work for instance, the authorities are already degrading the prisoner, which is tantamount to torture. Furthermore when that person leaves prison it is argued they won’t want to rehabilitate. As these minimum requirements are generally failed by the SA penal system, the country’s leadership in law enforcement and corrective institutions are not adhering to the spirit of non brutality of the Prevention and Combating of Torture of Persons Act. So starting with leadership, there appears to be a culture that seems to have been inculcated in SAPS which has to be rebuilt from the top down. Basically, police have to be reeducated about what it is to be a policeman. The Human Rights Commission has worked with District One police station in the Western Cape to provide alternative dignifying methodologies for handling crisis etc – which has led to turnaround. Another practical proposal for change is to introduce Body cams to be worn by all officers – to surveille the police, helping to police the actions of the police. We have filmed the scenes outside Eldorado Park SAPS on Friday 28 August, where locals were not only protesting Nathaniel Julies’s death, but also the arrest of Majiet Amiene who residents say was trying to calm the crowd when police fingered him. We have shot brief interviews with Amiene’s sisters and local campaigner Riaan __. We will interview Nathaniel Julies’s family, community leaders including Marcelle a special needs specialist in Eldorado Park, IPID and SAPS. We will also shoot further community protests or marches during the immediate fallout of Nathaniel Julies death.
